notes: Gentle opening (COURSE.md, owner 2026-11-08): section 1 introduces about ten opaque items (haben, pünktlich, Flasche/Rohr already met in a chapter-1 aid, Regel, trocken, zählen, Tisch, Ding, berühren), at most two per sentence, each with a one-word German aid in words already read; haben is fixed by gesture (Wolf holds a flask) before any form note.

Deferred chapter-1 words picked up here where the beats need them: schmutzig (clean/dirty glass), Wäscherin, Hemd/Hemden, dünn (thin glass breaks), Bub and gell (Kathrin's first dialect, each with its standard equivalent), arbeiten and kommen as present-tense verbs. Left for later: Hosen, übermorgen, dick, Brücke, Fluss, wohnt, Luft, froh, wichtig; Tuch and nass stay in their planned chapter 3.

Plan lexemes Morgen, Uhr, sagen and groß already exist from chapter 1: Uhr and groß are recycled; sagen (with waschen, sehen, heißen) is promoted from receptive to productive with its new present forms; the noun der Morgen takes id de-morgen-n because de-morgen is the chapter-1 adverb 'tomorrow' (plan row id collision; reconcile in plan maintenance).

Added study lexemes beyond the row, each used three or more times: Tisch, Abend (chapter-1 incidentals), Kreuzer, zwölf, zwanzig, acht, plus the deferred words above. Non-transparent new lexemes stay well under the 60 ceiling; Wasser, Sand, Schule, kosten and kaputt are flagged transparent.

Present narration, close third on Jakob. Address: Wolf and Kathrin du to Jakob; Jakob Sie to Wolf and the student, Herr Professor to Bunsen; Bunsen Er (3sg) to Jakob. The student says du to the servant boy.
Accusative objects (den Kolben, einen Kolben) and the chunk in der Kasse are bounded receptive incidentals before G03 (row incidental_allowed); none is a production answer.
Money: Baden reckoned 60 Kreuzer to the Gulden (chapter 1 used Gulden). The wage and flask prices are invented and kept plausible, not documented; see review questions.

Sol review round 1 (blocked) fixes: bounded the extra-e explanation to encountered forms (lernst, hält are exceptions); delivered a German-labelled shirt SVG for Hemden at s041 (de-NEW-01-l02-svg-hemd) instead of a category gloss; planted Wer in the story (s051) before Pensum C6; the student's order is now the indicative Du wäschst das. Schnell! (imperatives stay Wolf-only); replaced eight exercise items that copied story sentences; Rebellenbub kept as the plan-mandated compound with an owner question in OPEN.md.

Sol rounds 2–4: x4-2-2 recombined (Wolf antwortet ___ → leise) so no item copies a story sentence; s084 disposition recorded under the owner's register/voice delegation. Round 4 verdict: linguistically and pedagogically ready as a draft; wage, price, timetable and cash-box details remain explicitly invented.

Fresh-eyes fixes: x4-1-5 cue matches das Glas; x3-2-5 now asks for bezahle (ich), since the checker cannot accept the chapter-1 reading-only form zahlt as an answer; uncontracted von dem / in das reworded with taught forms (s017, s018, s039, s060); set-up clause for the other students before s084; x4-2-3 now a noun (Tisch). review_questions.question: [?] Wage and prices are invented: a boy's 12 Kreuzer a day (8 for afternoons) and 10/20 Kreuzer for a small/large laboratory flask in Heidelberg, 1852. Plausible orders of magnitude for Baden in the 1850s (a labourer earned roughly 30–48 Kreuzer a day), but not sourced.

[?] Schooling: Baden's elementary school obligation ran to about age 14, so a thirteen-year-old in a half-day arrangement (school mornings) is plausible; the morning/afternoon split is the card's agreement and is not claimed as a documented Heidelberg timetable.

[?] Source conflict (recorded in OPEN.md): the plan row and card require a student to call Jakob Rebellenbub, while COURSE.md reserves standalone Bub as Kathrin's marker. Disposition under the owner's 2026-11-08 delegation of register and voice to Claude (OWNER-SPEC.md, fourth round): the plan-mandated compound is a narrow exception, a coined insult rather than the student's dialect; no other character uses Bub, net or gell. Bub is first given by Kathrin (s046, = Junge) so the compound comes after its base word. The student also recognises Lauer from Mannheim as the printer, as Wolf did in chapter 1.

[?] Wolf pays 20 Kreuzer into 'die Kasse' (the laboratory's cash box) to replace the flask. The card says he pays quietly and tells Bunsen nothing; how a servant would actually settle a breakage is invented.

inference_aids.alt: Wolf shows Jakob how to wash the laboratory glass.
inference_aids.art_brief: Inside the cramped, smoky former Dominican monastery laboratory in Heidelberg, early morning in November 1852, grey light from a high window and one small yellow flame. Old Diener Wolf (grey, stooped, servant's apron, hands slightly trembling) holds up a dirty round-bottomed flask, black and yellow inside, over a stone washing basin of clear cold water with a heap of sand beside it. Jakob (13, thin, plain patched jacket, sleeves pushed up, clean hands) watches closely. On the left, clean dry glass stands upside down: flasks, bottles and long tubes; on the right, dirty glass waits. One large thin flask stands apart on a shelf. In the background a separate table with a cigar, papers and a prism: Bunsen's things, untouched. No text.

grammar.title: Grammatik
grammar.rule: Ich habe, du hast, er hat. Ich zähle, du zählst, er zählt. Jakob arbeitet. Arbeitet Jakob? Was kostet der Kolben?
grammar.note_en:
The present tense describes what happens now or usually. A German verb has a stem plus an ending that agrees with its subject. Take zählen (“to count”): the stem is zähl-. The endings met in this chapter are ich zähle (“I count”), du zählst (“you count”), er zählt (“he counts”), and -en for wir, for sie (“they”) and for polite Sie: Sie sagen nichts? (“You say nothing?”). Ihr, “you” to several people you each call du, takes -t: Seht ihr? (“Do you see?”). The full set is ich -e, du -st, er/sie/es -t, wir -en, ihr -t, sie/Sie -en. Some of the verbs here add an extra e before the ending: du arbeitest / er arbeitet (“you work / he works”), er kostet (“it costs”), du trocknest (“you dry”). It helps to pronounce the ending after a stem in -t or a stem like trockn-. Not every verb does this: lernen gives du lernst (“you learn”), without the e. Learn each form as you meet it.

Some common verbs change their vowel in the du and er forms only: waschen gives ich wasche but du wäschst, er wäscht (“washes”); brechen gives er bricht (“breaks”); sehen gives er sieht (“sees”); halten (“to hold”) gives er hält (“he holds”) and tragen (“to carry”) gives er trägt (“he carries”). Learn these with the verb. Haben (“to have”) is irregular: ich habe, du hast, er hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie/Sie haben. Ich habe am Morgen Schule means “I have school in the morning”. Sein (“to be”) is also irregular: ich bin, du bist, er ist, wir/sie/Sie sind.

Questions. In a yes/no question the finite verb (the verb form with the ending) comes first: Wasche ich auch? (“Do I wash too?”), Habt ihr da Feuer? (“Do you have fire there?”). German has no helper like English “do”. With a question word, the question word comes first and the verb second: Was kostet ein Kolben? (“What does a flask cost?”), Was hast du? (“What do you have?”), Wie heißt du? (“What is your name?”), Wer bezahlt die Miete? (“Who pays the rent?”). In a statement the verb is the second constituent, as in chapter 1. If something other than the subject comes first, the subject follows the verb: Am Abend zählst du die Kolben (“In the evening you count the flasks”); Dann trocknest du das Glas (“Then you dry the glass”).

Address. Du is “you” for a child, family or a friend: Wolf and Kathrin say du to Jakob. Sie (with a capital, and with the -en form) is “you” for an adult you respect: Jakob says Sie to Wolf and to the student, Sie haben Geld (“You have money”). Bunsen uses the old Er to the boy: Ist Er schnell? (“Are you fast?”), Zählt Er das Glas? (“Do you count the glass?”). Er takes the third-person singular ending, like er, but it means “you”. It belonged to masters speaking to servants and children in the nineteenth century; do not use it today.

Reading chunks, not yet patterns: the student's Du wäschst das. Schnell! (“You'll wash that. Quickly!”) uses an ordinary present tense as a blunt order. After verbs such as waschen, haben and bezahlen, masculine der changes to den and ein to einen: Wolf wäscht den Kolben (“Wolf washes the flask”), Wolf hat einen Kolben (“Wolf has a flask”). This is the accusative case, the form for the object, taught in chapter 3. Nicht often goes to the end of a short sentence: Du berührst die Dinge von Professor Bunsen nicht (“You don't touch Professor Bunsen's things”). Wolf says to Bunsen Der Junge berührt Ihre Dinge nicht (“The boy does not touch your things”): Ihre is the polite “your”, as Ihr in chapter 1. Morgen (small m) is “tomorrow”; der Morgen (capital M) is “the morning”: am Morgen, am Nachmittag, am Abend mean “in the morning / afternoon / evening”; am Tag means “a day” or “per day”: zwölf Kreuzer am Tag (“twelve kreuzer a day”). Zu schnell means “too fast”; zu also means “closed” (Die Tür ist zu). Kathrin is from the Palatinate: she says Bub for Junge (“boy”) and gell? for “isn't it? / right?” at the end of a sentence. These are regional words, and in this book only Kathrin uses them as her own speech. The student's Rebellenbub (“rebel's boy”) is a compound of Rebell and Bub, coined as an insult; German builds compounds by joining words, and the last part names the thing. Money: Baden counted in Gulden; 60 Kreuzer made one Gulden.

items.prompt: Was kostet der Kolben dort, und was ist der Lohn von Jakob?
model_answers: Der Kolben kostet zwanzig Kreuzer. Der Lohn ist zwölf Kreuzer.
items.rubric: Twenty kreuzer for the large flask; twelve kreuzer a day (later eight, for afternoons only, is also correct).

items.prompt: Was ist Kathrin, und was wäscht sie?

items.prompt: Jakob hat jetzt Schule. Was ist der Lohn jetzt?

items.prompt: Was sagt der Student, und was antwortet Jakob?
